name: json.cpp
workload: Parsing and serializing JSON test fixtures (object_test, deep_test, parse_test, round_trip_test, json_test_suite), each run 2000x, comparing json.cpp to nlohmann::ordered_json
claimed_speedup: ~2.85x faster parsing (675ns vs 1928ns on parse_test), 2.9x on deep_test (226ns vs 659ns), 3.25x on round_trip_test (1309ns vs 4258ns), 1.6x on json_test_suite (10462ns vs 16617ns); also ~10x faster compile time (~120ms vs 1200ms+) and ~100x fewer source lines (233 vs 24,766)
tradeoffs: Far smaller feature/API surface than nlohmann::json (233 vs ~24.7k lines); newer and much less battle-tested; API is not drop-in compatible with nlohmann's
caveats: First-party benchmark run by the author on the author's own hardware; no independent reproduction found. The author's own README flags that json_test_suite() shows an unexplained 39x gap on one sub-metric ('we haven't figured out how to explain yet'), so treat headline ratios with some caution even though compiler/flags/CPU are fully disclosed and benchmark code ships in-repo.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "JSON C++ library benchmark faster than std::format std::stringstream" surfaced jart/json.cpp

name: scnlib
workload: Parsing an integer, a floating-point number, and a whitespace-delimited word/string from text input, comparing scn::scan to std::stringstream and libc sscanf
claimed_speedup: Integer parse: 27.1ns (scn::scan) vs 85.5ns (stringstream) vs 272.7ns (sscanf); float parse: 59.7ns vs 283ns vs 432ns; string/word parse: 24.5ns vs 134ns vs 58.4ns — roughly 3-5x faster than std::stringstream across cases
tradeoffs: Requires adopting scn's scan-based API instead of iostream/scanf idioms; adds a library/header dependency; format-string parsing has its own learning curve; gains are largest for CPU-bound parsing, smaller for I/O-bound workloads
caveats: Numbers are from the project's own in-repo benchmark suite (built via the SCN_BENCHMARKS CMake option), dated 2024-05-23 in the README; not independently reproduced by a third party. Whether std::stringstream was backed by libstdc++ or libc++ isn't stated.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "scnlib benchmark faster than std::istream sscanf github"

name: Cap'n Proto
workload: Serializing/deserializing a fixed trading-domain object graph (accounts, balances, orders) in chronoxor/CppSerialization's multi-protocol shootout
claimed_speedup: 247ns serialize / 184ns deserialize (Cap'n Proto, 208 bytes) vs 696ns serialize / 291ns deserialize (JSON via RapidJSON, 301 bytes) — ~2.8x faster serialize, ~1.6x faster deserialize (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Release build; exact compiler version/flags not stated in the README
tradeoffs: Requires a .capnp schema and code-generation step; wire format is not human-readable, unlike JSON; zero-copy design changes idiomatic usage vs building strings/streams by hand
caveats: Numbers come from a third-party shootout repo (chronoxor/CppSerialization), not Cap'n Proto's own benchmarks; exact compiler and optimization flags aren't stated (only "Release build"), which is why this falls short of Tier A. The JSON side of the comparison used RapidJSON, not raw iostream/std::string formatting.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "Cap'n Proto benchmark vs Protocol Buffers JSON serialization speed numbers CPU"

name: zpp::bits
workload: Same trading-domain object-graph benchmark as above, from chronoxor/CppSerialization's multi-protocol shootout
claimed_speedup: 34ns serialize / 37ns deserialize (zpp::bits, 130 bytes) vs 696ns serialize / 291ns deserialize (JSON via RapidJSON, 301 bytes) — ~20x faster serialize, ~7.9x faster deserialize (derived from page data)
compiler_and_flags: Release build; exact compiler version/flags not stated in the README
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 library with no schema/codegen, but needs aggregate/structured-binding-friendly types; output is a compact binary format, not JSON-compatible or human-readable; SimpleBinaryEncoding had an even smaller message size in the same shootout, so the 'winner' depends on which metric (speed vs size) matters most
caveats: Numbers come from a third-party shootout repo, not zpp::bits's own benchmark; compiler version/flags beyond "Release build" are not stated. This was the fastest of several binary formats in that shootout, all of which beat the RapidJSON/JSON baseline by wide margins.
found_via: GitHub: harvested as the top-performing winner from the chronoxor/CppSerialization shootout

name: blazingio
workload: Reading/writing integers, floating-point numbers, strings, complex numbers, and bitsets via a cin/cout-compatible API, compared to libstdc++ iostream
claimed_speedup: ~5x faster than libstdc++ iostream (with sync_with_stdio(false)) across integer/string/float I/O primitives
hardware: 64-bit Linux; exact CPU model not stated
tradeoffs: Targets competitive-programming use (whole-input buffering, exceptions off, etc.); only a subset of iostream semantics is drop-in compatible; no libc++ or MSVC STL comparison given, only libstdc++
caveats: First-party README claim. Benchmark code and a linked raw-data spreadsheet exist, but the CPU model isn't named in the README, so per the evidence-tier rules this is capped at C rather than A/B despite the compiler/OS being named.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "serialization library faster than iostream stringstream benchmark C++"

name: HPS (High Performance Serialization)
workload: Serializing common STL containers and user-defined types (including a sparse matrix), compared against Boost Serialization, Protocol Buffers, and Cap'n Proto
claimed_speedup: Up to 150% faster (~2.5x) and up to 40% smaller output than Boost Serialization for several common data structures; beats Cap'n Proto in all tested cases except the sparse-matrix workload
tradeoffs: No IDL/schema like Protobuf or Cap'n Proto (works directly on STL/user types via templates), so less cross-language tooling; unmaintained for years, may need patching to build with modern compilers
caveats: Claim appears in an arXiv preprint (arXiv:1811.04556) and the project README/benchmark code (src/benchmark); compiler, flags, and hardware for the runs are not stated in the repo, and the paper does not appear to have gone through formal peer review, so this is capped at Tier C rather than B.
found_via: GitHub: WebSearch "HPS high performance serialization library C++ github faster than boost protobuf capnproto"
